title: The Healing at Bethesda and the Son Who Works Like the Father
summary: At a pool in Jerusalem Jesus heals a man who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years, telling him to pick up his mat and walk on the Sabbath. When the religious authorities object, Jesus answers that he is working as his Father works, and they seek to kill him for making himself equal with God. The rest of the chapter is Jesus' long defense: the Son gives life and judges with the Father's authority, and a whole line of witnesses testifies to him.
story: The first four chapters of John have been mostly welcome and wonder: the wine at Cana, Nicodemus by night, the Samaritan woman, the official's son healed at a distance. Chapter 5 is the turning point. For the first time a sign provokes open hostility, and for the first time we read that the authorities wanted to kill Jesus (5:18). From here the Gospel moves under a gathering shadow. The chapter also sets the pattern for the chapters that follow: a sign, a controversy, and then a discourse in which Jesus explains what the sign means about who he is. Much of what John will say about the Father and the Son is first laid out here.
historical:
Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for an unnamed feast of the Jews (5:1). Interpreters have proposed Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles, and Purim, and the text doesn't settle it. The pool called Bethesda (some manuscripts read Bethzatha) stood north of the temple near the Sheep Gate. Excavations near the Church of St. Anne in Jerusalem uncovered a large double pool whose shape suits John's description of five colonnades: four around the edges and one across the middle. For a long time some critics treated John's detail as symbolic invention, and the discovery has made many more willing to credit the Gospel's knowledge of Jerusalem before AD 70. Remains from the Roman period at the site suggest it was later a healing sanctuary, possibly dedicated to the Greek healing god Asclepius, though what it was in Jesus' day is less certain.

The opponents are called simply the Jews. In John's Gospel the Greek word Ioudaioi can mean Jews in general, Judeans (people of Judea as distinct from Galilee), or, very often, the religious authorities in Jerusalem. Here it plainly means the last: the people who question the healed man, who can persecute Jesus, and who plan his death are the leaders around the temple, not the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus himself, his disciples, and the healed man are all Jews. That distinction matters because these passages were later used by Christians to blame the Jewish people collectively for the death of Jesus, a charge that fed centuries of contempt, expulsions, and violence and was exploited in modern antisemitic propaganda. The Roman Catholic Church formally rejected the charge of collective Jewish guilt in its 1965 declaration Nostra Aetate, and most churches now read John with this history in view.
cultural:
The Sabbath, the seventh day of rest commanded in the Ten Commandments, was one of the chief marks of Jewish identity in the Roman world. The commandment forbade work but didn't define it, so teachers worked out what counted. The Mishnah, a collection of rabbinic rulings written down about AD 200 but preserving older tradition, lists thirty-nine categories of forbidden work; the last is carrying an object from one domain to another. Carrying a mat through the city fell under that concern, which is why the authorities object to the man before they ask about his healing.

Jewish teachers also recognized that God himself doesn't stop working on the Sabbath: he keeps the world in being, gives life, and judges. Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher contemporary with Jesus, said that God never ceases making. Jesus' reply in 5:17 builds on that shared conviction and then applies it to himself, which is exactly why his hearers understood him to be claiming equality with God. Verse 4, which describes an angel stirring the water so that the first one in was healed, is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and is omitted in the BSB. Verse 7 does show that people believed the stirred water had healing power.
literary: The chapter has two movements: a short healing story (5:1-18) and a long speech (5:19-47). The healing is told with irony. The man never asks for healing, never learns Jesus' name at first, and reports Jesus to the authorities afterward. The speech opens with the solemn double amen, “Truly, truly, I tell you” (5:19), repeated three times in the first part. It then turns into something like a courtroom argument. Jewish law required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and Jesus concedes that his own word alone would not stand (5:31). He calls his witnesses in turn: John the Baptist, the works the Father gave him, the Father himself, and the Scriptures, with Moses as the final witness who becomes the accuser. The trial theme runs through the whole Gospel; here the accused becomes the judge.

outline.t: Jesus heals the invalid at the pool of Bethesda
The Sabbath controversy and the claim of equality with God
The Son gives life and judges with the Father's authority
The witnesses: John, the works, the Father, the Scriptures
Seeking glory from people, and Moses as accuser

doctrines.note: The Son does nothing on his own but only what he sees the Father doing, and yet “whatever the Father does, the Son also does” (5:19). John holds together real distinction and full unity: the Son is sent and obedient, and he is also to be honored “just as they honor the Father” (5:23). The church's later language of one God in three persons grew from passages like this.

The Father “has assigned all judgment to the Son” (5:22). Judgment is both future, when all in their graves will hear his voice (5:28-29), and already under way, since whoever believes “has crossed over from death to life” (5:24).
Jesus says the Scriptures are “the very words that testify about Me” (5:39). Reading the Bible diligently is not the same as hearing it; its purpose is to lead the reader to the one it points toward.

words.note: Ergazomai, to work. In 5:17 Jesus uses it of both the Father and himself: the Father is working to this day, and so is he. The word ties the healing to God's ongoing work of sustaining and giving life, which even the Sabbath doesn't interrupt. John uses the related noun ergon, work, for Jesus' deeds throughout the Gospel.

Isos, equal. The narrator explains the authorities' fury: Jesus was “calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God” (5:18). The rest of the chapter doesn't deny the charge but explains it: the Son's equality is not a rival claim to independence but a perfect sharing in the Father's work.

Martureō, to testify or bear witness. It appears seven times in this chapter, and the related noun marturia four more. Witness is one of John's central themes; the Gospel presents itself as testimony, and here Jesus summons witnesses as in a trial.

Krisis, judgment. The word can mean a legal verdict or the act of judging, and sometimes condemnation. In John it carries both senses: the Son has authority to judge, and the one who believes “will not come under judgment” (5:24), meaning condemnation.

christ: This chapter is one of the New Testament's fullest statements of who Jesus is in relation to God. He gives life as the Father gives life (5:21). He has “life in Himself” (5:26), something said of God alone. He will raise the dead with his voice (5:28). He is the Son of Man of Daniel 7, given authority to judge (5:27). And he is also the Son who does nothing by himself, who seeks not his own will but the will of the one who sent him (5:30). John's portrait refuses to make Jesus either a lesser god or a mere prophet. The healing of a man who could not walk for thirty-eight years becomes a small picture of what the Son does: he speaks, and those who cannot help themselves get up.

hard.q: Does John's language about “the Jews” make the Gospel anti-Jewish?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real. John uses the term Ioudaioi about seventy times, often for those who oppose Jesus, and later Christians used these passages to justify hostility toward Jewish people. Readers have responded in several ways. Many scholars note that the term frequently means the Judean religious leadership, not the people as a whole, and that John also uses it neutrally or positively (4:22 says salvation is from the Jews, and many Jews believe in Jesus in chapters 11 and 12). Others, such as J. Louis Martyn, argued that the Gospel's sharp tone reflects a later painful conflict between Jewish followers of Jesus and synagogue leaders, and so it records an argument within a Jewish family rather than a verdict on a people. Still others think no single explanation removes the difficulty and that the church must read these texts with repentance for how they have been used.

What the text itself shows is that every main character in the story is Jewish, including Jesus, and that the opposition comes from a particular leadership in a particular place and time. To turn this into a charge against a people is a misreading, and one with a long and grievous history.

questions: Jesus asks the man, “Do you want to get well?” Why might someone not want healing, or not know how to answer that question?
The man reports Jesus to the authorities. What does his response suggest about the difference between being helped by Jesus and trusting him?
Jesus says the Scriptures testify about him, yet his hearers studied them and missed him. How can careful study of the Bible miss its point?
